items.title: ZML releases LLMD alpha, a cross-platform LLM inference server supporting NVIDIA, AMD, Google TPU, Intel, and Apple Metal architectures with modern serving features [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ZML/LLMD alpha – cross platform LLM server
items.summary:
ZML has launched LLMD alpha, a self-contained inference server that runs large language models like LLaMa, Gemma, Qwen, and Mistral across five hardware architectures including NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, Google TPU, Intel oneAPI, and Apple Metal. The server supports features such as continuous batching, paged attention, tensor parallel sharding, prefix caching, and tool calling, and exposes metrics in Prometheus format.

LLMD alpha includes native support for loading models directly from HuggingFace, S3, and Google Cloud Storage without prior downloading, using ZML's virtual file system. It also introduces DFlash speculative decoding for certain models, which can speed up token processing by up to 10 times. The server ships with optimized Docker images tailored for each platform, including built-in CUDA compatibility and automatic tensor parallel sharding across devices. LLMD runs on ZML's own ML framework built with Zig, MLIR, and OpenXLA, providing predictable latency and a Python-free execution path.

items.originalTitle: Show HN: Rowboat – Open-source, local-first alternative to Claude Desktop
items.summary:
Rowboat is an open-source desktop AI assistant that indexes your work into a living knowledge graph to help manage tasks on your machine. It includes built-in interfaces for email, notes, browsing, coding, meeting notes, and project workspaces, all stored locally as editable Markdown files without proprietary lock-in.

The tool supports integration with various external services and APIs, including Google services, voice input/output, web search, and productivity tools via the Model Context Protocol. Users can bring their own AI models, either local or hosted, and swap them without losing data, emphasizing privacy and long-term memory accumulation rather than reconstructing context on demand.

items.title: Tarit launches a self-hosted microVM hypervisor and sandbox cloud for AI agents with fast, secure, ephemeral environments and multi-node orchestration [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Tarit – Self-host sandbox cloud and hypervisor for AI agents
items.summary:
Tarit is a microVM platform designed to provide secure, fast, and ephemeral sandbox environments for AI agents and reinforcement learning workloads. It uses hardware virtualization to create isolated microVMs with their own kernels, enabling real isolation and rapid boot times in milliseconds. The platform includes a minimal Rust-based hypervisor and a multi-node orchestrator that manages microVM fleets with features like placement, warm pools, networking, snapshots, and usage auditing.

The system supports snapshotting, suspend/resume, and live snapshots for efficient VM state management, and exposes a Unix-domain socket protocol for control plane integration. Tarit is built for Linux hosts with KVM support and offers a layered quickstart for running code in microVMs, managing snapshots, and operating fleets via an HTTP API and SSH gateway. It aims to provide a secure and efficient infrastructure for running AI workloads in isolated, ephemeral environments.

items.title: Developer builds AI-powered code review system using OpenAI Codex to integrate with existing workflows and measure review effectiveness [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Making AI Code Review Measurable
items.summary:
A software engineer at loveholidays developed an AI-assisted code review tool leveraging OpenAI's Codex to run reviews within existing workflows, aiming to make code review processes measurable and more effective. The system clones pull requests, analyzes code context beyond diffs, and outputs structured JSON reviews to facilitate evaluation and integration.

The developer tested the tool using past pull requests as fixtures to simulate real review scenarios, incorporating feedback from colleagues to refine the evaluation criteria. This approach allowed assessment of the AI's ability to approve or reject code changes based on historical outcomes, helping to quantify the impact of AI in code review without relying on costly subscriptions or external tools.

This alternative successfully processes and summarizes lengthy voice notes privately, demonstrating that flagship AI models are not always the best fit for specific on-device applications.

items.originalTitle: Mews Cuts 15% of Staff, Points to AI in Broad Restructuring
items.summary:
Mews, a hotel software company serving over 15,000 hotels worldwide, has laid off 15% of its approximately 1,350 employees in its largest restructuring since the pandemic. CEO Richard Valtr attributed the cuts to AI making many roles obsolete, as the company aims to transition from selling software to providing AI services that handle hotel tasks like revenue management and procurement.

The layoffs affected about 170 roles across all teams and locations, sparing most customer-facing positions. This move reflects a broader trend in travel technology companies, such as Expedia and Amex GBT, which are also restructuring their workforce while investing in AI capabilities.

OpenAI is releasing its GPT-5.6 models on Thursday following a delay imposed by the U.S. government, which lifted restrictions after additional testing by the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The company criticized the hold, saying it delayed access to advanced tools for developers and businesses, while binding standards for AI model releases remain absent despite recent executive orders.

The electronics conglomerate may be best known in the U.S. for its TV sets and smartphones, which jostle with the iPhone for attention, but it’s also one of the three biggest makers of memory chips globally (along with Micron Technology and SK Hynix). The explosion of that business, thanks to demand from AI data centers, has turbocharged profits at all three companies—with Samsung providing fresh evidence of that on Tuesday.

Samsung issued a “pre-earnings guidance” notification—which we usually see from companies about to drop bad news they think investors need to hear as soon as possible—that its second-quarter operating profit would be about 89.4 trillion Korean won, or $59 billion. That would be up 1,800% on the year-earlier operating profit of just $3.1 billion. That’s even better than the 1,435% growth Micron reported in its operating profit a couple of weeks ago for the May quarter. Hynix, which is planning to list on the Nasdaq later this week, hasn’t yet reported for the second quarter. (Ironically, investors sold Samsung stock 7% down on Tuesday, apparently expecting even better growth—some people are never satisfied.)

items.originalTitle: The Prolonged Write-Downs in Enterprise Software Startups
items.summary:
It’s not easy to run an enterprise software company these days. For the nth example of this, read the latest story by my colleague Laura Bratton, who describes how an Atlanta real estate manager replaced Salesforce software with a custom app developed using Replit and Claude Code—saving $100,000 a year. Yipes. 

Fears that companies will replace their software subscriptions with cheaper AI tools have hammered not just publicly traded stocks but the valuations of private companies. While we don’t often get a look at these private valuations unless the startups sell more shares, mutual fund disclosures give a glimpse into how big public investors are feeling. As the attached chart shows, for most it’s pretty bleak.

items.title: Facing a Revolt, HubSpot Reverses Decision to Use Customer Data For AI Feature [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Facing a Revolt, HubSpot Reverses Decision to Use Customer Data For AI Feature
items.summary:
HubSpot last week triggered a firestorm among customers after announcing a plan to use some of the data they store with HubSpot’s customer relationship management app to power a forthcoming AI-powered feature.

While HubSpot reversed course four days later, the episode shows how sensitive customers are to software firms using their data in the AI era. HubSpot’s reversal is also another demonstration of the leverage that businesses have with the traditional software firms nowadays. We've noted before that some large customers have been able to shorten their contracts with software firms, which are keen not to lose clients given fears of rising competition from AI companies.

Let’s get back to HubSpot, whose shares are down 75% since early last year on fears AI would hurt its business and whose executives said sales growth would be slightly slower this year compared to last year.

On July 1, HubSpot announced it would use some customer data for a new AI feature that helps customers find new sales leads, which was set to launch next month.

HubSpot told customers in an email that it would collect such data by default and that customers would have to manually cut off access if they didn’t want Hubspot collecting it. HubSpot also said it may share their data, including “business contact details, employer information, and email deliverability signals,” with other customers. (HubSpot also said it had updated its terms of service, privacy policy and other customer agreements to reflect the change in its data collection practices.)
